content_units: Four-Month Course Fit Snapshot

With    128 hours available   over 4 months at   8 hours/week  , both courses fit on paper, but   Course A is the stronger match   for your goal of landing an   entry-level data analyst job quickly while working full time  .
Best fit:   Course A
- Better aligned to common entry-level analyst requirements:   Excel + SQL + Tableau + portfolio
- Lower cost:   EUR 420
- Uses your existing Excel strength while directly fixing your   weak SQL gap
- More job-ready in 4 months than starting from zero in Python
Course-to-Goal Comparison
Option   Total Time   Weekly Load Over 4 Months   Core Skills   Career Fit for Entry-Level Analyst   Main Trade-off
Course A   120 hours   7.5 hrs/week   Excel, SQL, Tableau, portfolio project     High     Less Python/statistics depth
Course B   80 hours   5 hrs/week   Python, pandas, statistics, capstone   Medium   Misses SQL and BI/dashboard emphasis
Best choice   120 hours   Fits your 8 hrs/week   Job-ready analyst stack     Course A     Add light Python later
Recommended Choice and Why
Course A
Course A is the better fit because it optimizes for your stated priorities in order:
-   Get job-ready within 4 months:   SQL and Tableau show up more often than Python for many junior analyst roles.
-   Work around a full-time schedule:   120 hours across 16 weeks is manageable at   7.5 hours/week  , leaving a small buffer.
-   Build on current strengths:   Since your Excel is already strong, you can likely move faster there and spend more effort on SQL and portfolio quality.
-   Improve hiring readiness:   A visible   portfolio project   is especially useful for entry-level applications.
Trade-off alternative: Course B
Course B is better only if you want to steer toward a more technical analytics path later and are comfortable being   less directly aligned to typical analyst job postings in the short term  .
- Stronger for future automation and data wrangling
- Better if you specifically want to learn Python early
- Weaker immediate fit because you would still lack   SQL depth   and likely   dashboard tooling
Skills Gap After Finishing Course A
If you complete   Course A  , your likely remaining gaps would be:
-   Python fundamentals
- You would still be behind candidates who can use pandas for cleaning and analysis.
-   Deeper statistics
- Enough for reporting, but likely not enough for stronger analytical testing/modeling tasks.
-   Advanced SQL
- Depending on course depth, you may still need more practice with joins, CTEs, window functions, and query optimization.
-   Business case storytelling
- One portfolio project helps, but you may still need   1–2 more polished projects   tailored to real business questions.
-   Job search assets
- Resume bullets, LinkedIn positioning, GitHub/portfolio presentation, and interview practice are usually still needed.
Most important gap to close after Course A
Python basics   would be the main remaining gap, but it is a   secondary gap   for many entry-level analyst roles compared with SQL and dashboarding.
Practical 4-Month Outcome
A realistic outcome from   Course A + disciplined weekly practice  :
- You become employable for junior roles that ask for:
- Excel
- SQL
- dashboards/BI
- basic business analysis
- You may still be weaker for roles emphasizing:
- Python-heavy analytics
- experimentation/statistics depth
- data science-style workflows
Quick Actions
Choose Course AAdd Python Later
Decision Context
I assumed:
- “Entry-level data analyst job” means the shortest path to   interview-ready skills  , not long-term specialization.
- Your 8 hours/week is fairly consistent across the full 4 months.
- Neither course includes substantial extra career support beyond what you listed.
